vignette:
# Karim's Vigilance

Karim was thirty-seven years old when his father's fists came through the kitchen wall. He remembers the drywall dust hanging in the air like fog, remembers his mother's face—the particular angle of her cheekbone as she turned away—remembers the sound of his own breathing, which seemed impossibly loud. He does not remember what started it. When he tries to reconstruct the sequence now, at forty-one, sitting in a construction trailer during his lunch break, the beginning dissolves. There is the wall. There is his mother's silence afterward. There is the space between those two moments that simply will not come into focus, no matter how hard he concentrates.

What remains instead are the sensations. The smell of plaster. The way his father's shoulders moved when he was about to strike—a specific tightening that Karim learned to read the way other children learned to read letters. The knowledge, crystalline and immediate, that sound would follow violence, and that his job was to make himself small. He was nine. By eleven, he had become expert at reading the micro-expressions in his father's face, the tension in a room before anyone else could feel it coming. By fifteen, when his father finally left, Karim had already spent years convinced that his own safety depended on his ability to predict danger in the bodies of men around him.

The intervening years had taught him a kind of peace, or what he had mistaken for peace. He built things. Framing, drywall, concrete foundations—work that was methodical and visible. He could see what he had made. He did not have to think about what was coming next. For a long time, he did not.

But three years ago, a police cruiser pulled into the construction site where Karim was working. A routine inspection, someone said. Routine. The officer was young, polite even, but the moment Karim saw the uniform and the belt—the specific configuration of authority and potential violence—his body moved before his mind caught up. His hands began to shake. His heart accelerated into a rhythm that felt dangerous. He could not explain it. The officer had done nothing. But Karim's chest was tight, his breath shallow, and he was certain—absolutely certain—that something terrible was about to happen. He left the site early, told his foreman he was sick.

That was when things began to narrow. He started to avoid the morning meetings where his supervisor discussed upcoming projects and timelines. Talking about the future, about what would happen next week or next month, sent him into a state of dread he could not articulate. What if something went wrong? What if he could not control what came next? It was easier to stop engaging. His foreman noticed. There were conversations about Karim's commitment, his reliability. He was moved to solo jobs whenever possible, which suited him fine. Fewer people. Fewer surprises.

When disagreements arose on the job site—a subcontractor questioning his measurements, a homeowner wanting changes mid-project—Karim simply agreed to everything. It was not worth the risk of confrontation. The moment someone's voice rose, or their face shifted into what he read as anger, his body flooded with the same panic that the police officer had triggered. He would feel his father's shoulders tightening all over again. He would retreat. He would say yes to whatever was being asked, even when it was unreasonable, even when it meant redoing work or absorbing costs that were not his responsibility.

In the evenings, when he was alone in his apartment, Karim sometimes found himself lost in elaborate fantasies about who he used to be. There was a version of himself from before—before his father's violence had become the organizing principle of his nervous system—that felt almost real when he let himself drift into it. In those moments, he was competent, unafraid, capable of holding his ground. He would sit on his couch for hours, not quite asleep, not quite awake, moving through these imagined versions of himself until the evening was gone.

The memories of that day in the kitchen were strange. Some details were impossibly vivid: the exact shade of white on the wall, the sound of his mother's breath catching. But when he tried deliberately to remember the sequence, to piece together what had happened and why, the narrative would scatter. It was as if his mind had photographed individual moments and then locked them in separate rooms, refusing to let him walk through the door that connected them.

Last month, his sister called to tell him she was getting married. She wanted to know if he would come to the engagement party, if he would meet her fiancé's family, if he would help with planning. The questions arrived like a cascade of small explosions. Future. Confrontation. Authority figures he would not know. Expectations he could not control. He told her he would think about it. He has not called her back. Instead, he has begun to wonder if this is simply who he is now—a man who reads threat in every face, who cannot imagine a future that does not terrify him, who has become so practiced at disappearing that he is not sure anyone would notice if he stopped showing up at all.

It was his sister's persistence, her refusal to let him vanish, that finally pushed him to call a therapist. She had said something that landed: "You're still hiding from Dad, and he's been gone for twenty-six years." He is not sure if she is right. But he knows that something has to change, because the version of himself he has been protecting—the small, vigilant boy—is all that is left.
